passages.title: The Great Fire of London
passages.text:
In the small hours of Sunday, 2 September 1666, a fire broke out in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane in the heart of London. At first no one was greatly alarmed, for fires were common in a city built almost entirely of timber and thatch. But that summer had been long and dry, and a strong east wind was blowing. Within hours the flames had leapt from house to house, and the narrow, crowded streets became rivers of fire.

The Lord Mayor, woken and asked to pull down houses to make a firebreak, is said to have grumbled that a woman might put the blaze out, and gone back to bed. It was a costly mistake. For four days the fire raged, driving thousands of families from their homes. People fled to the river, piling their belongings into boats, while others buried their treasures in their gardens. The diarist Samuel Pepys famously buried his wine and a parmesan cheese to save them from the flames.

By the time the wind at last dropped and the fire was halted, much of the old city lay in ashes. More than thirteen thousand houses and old St Paul's Cathedral had been destroyed, yet remarkably few people are known to have died. From the ruins a new London slowly rose, built more in brick and stone than in wood, and the great cathedral we know today was designed by Sir Christopher Wren to stand where the old one had fallen.
passages.source_note: Original work written for this pack (an informative recount of the Great Fire of London, 1666).

questions.stem: Where did the Great Fire of London break out?

options.text: inside St Paul's Cathedral
in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane
on a boat on the river
in the Lord Mayor's house
in a bakery on Bread Street

questions.explanation: The fire 'broke out in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane'.

questions.stem: In which year did the Great Fire take place?
questions.explanation: The passage dates the fire to 2 September 1666.

questions.stem: What did Samuel Pepys bury to save it from the fire?

options.text: his diary and letters
his gold and silver coins
his books and papers
his best furniture
his wine and a parmesan cheese

questions.explanation: Pepys 'famously buried his wine and a parmesan cheese'.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did the fire spread so quickly at first?

options.text: the firefighters were away on holiday
there was no water anywhere in London
the city was built of timber and thatch, and a strong wind was blowing
the fire started in many places at once
the streets were far too wide

questions.explanation: A city of timber and thatch, a long dry summer and a strong east wind let the flames race from house to house.

questions.stem: How many houses does the passage say were destroyed?

options.text: more than thirteen thousand
more than three hundred
exactly one thousand
more than thirty thousand
fewer than one hundred

questions.explanation: The passage states 'more than thirteen thousand houses' were destroyed.

questions.stem: Why were fires 'common' in London at that time?

options.text: people lit fires for fun
most buildings were made of wood and thatch, which catch fire easily
there were no fire services anywhere in the world
the weather in London was always hot
the river itself often caught fire

questions.explanation: A city built 'almost entirely of timber and thatch' catches fire easily, so fires were common.

questions.stem: What does the Lord Mayor's reaction suggest about him?

options.text: he was a brave and quick-thinking leader
he had already put out many great fires
he was frightened of the baker
he secretly wanted the city to burn
he badly underestimated how serious the fire was

questions.explanation: Grumbling that a woman could put it out and going back to bed shows he failed to grasp the danger.

questions.stem: Why did people pile their belongings into boats and bury their treasures?

options.text: they were moving house that week anyway
they were playing a street game
they were desperately trying to save their possessions from the flames
they wanted to sell their things at the river
they were hiding from the Lord Mayor

questions.explanation: With the fire spreading, Londoners rushed to save whatever they could from the flames.

questions.stem: The passage says 'remarkably few people are known to have died'. The word 'remarkably' suggests the writer finds this:

options.text: sad and disappointing
surprising, given how huge and destructive the fire was
completely expected
of no importance at all
hard to believe and probably untrue

questions.explanation: 'Remarkably' signals the writer's surprise that so vast a fire cost so few lives.

questions.stem: Why was the new London built 'more in brick and stone than in wood'?

options.text: because all the wood had run out
because brick was much cheaper
to make the city far less likely to catch fire again
to make the city look older
because the king wanted it purely for beauty

questions.explanation: Having seen a timber city burn, builders used brick and stone, which do not catch fire so easily.

questions.stem: In 'the flames had leapt from house to house', the word 'leapt' suggests the fire moved:

options.text: slowly and steadily
quietly and gently
backwards down the street
in one straight line
quickly and suddenly

questions.explanation: 'Leapt' pictures the fire jumping swiftly and suddenly from one building to the next.

questions.stem: The passage says the fire 'raged' for four days. Here 'raged' means the fire:

options.text: died down slowly
smouldered quietly
burned violently and out of control
burned neatly in one spot
spread politely and slowly

questions.explanation: To 'rage' is to burn with great, uncontrolled fury.

questions.stem: A 'firebreak', made by pulling down houses, is meant to:

options.text: stop the fire from moving any further
make the fire burn hotter
give the firefighters a rest
provide a road for carts
mark where the fire began

questions.explanation: A firebreak is a gap with nothing to burn, so the fire cannot cross it.

questions.stem: The Lord Mayor is said to have 'grumbled'. To 'grumble' is to:

options.text: shout with joy
complain in a low, discontented way
laugh out loud
whisper a secret
sing cheerfully

questions.explanation: 'Grumbling' is muttering complaints -- here, that the fire was not worth his trouble.

questions.stem: 'Much of the old city lay in ashes.' Here 'lay in ashes' means the city was:

options.text: covered in deep snow
flooded with river water
left perfectly safe
freshly rebuilt
burnt to the ground

questions.explanation: To 'lie in ashes' is to be burned down to nothing but ash.

questions.stem: The narrow streets are called 'rivers of fire'. This is an example of:

options.text: a simile
personification
alliteration
onomatopoeia
a metaphor

questions.explanation: The streets are said to BE rivers of fire, without using 'like' or 'as', which makes it a metaphor.

questions.stem: Describing the burning streets as flowing rivers helps the reader picture the fire as:

options.text: pouring and flowing through the streets like water
putting the flames out with water
small and easy to step across
cold and slow-moving
flooding the streets with rain

questions.explanation: The image of a river makes us see the fire pouring and streaming along the streets, unstoppable as a flood.

questions.stem: Which of these happened FIRST?

options.text: a fire broke out in a baker's shop
the new London was rebuilt in brick
old St Paul's Cathedral was destroyed
the Lord Mayor went back to bed
families fled to the river

questions.explanation: The passage begins with the outbreak in the baker's shop; everything else follows from it.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the second paragraph?

options.text: to explain exactly where the fire started
to describe the building of the new city
to list the scientific causes of fire
to describe how people reacted as the fire took hold
to describe St Paul's Cathedral in detail

questions.explanation: The second paragraph moves from the Lord Mayor's blunder to how ordinary Londoners fled and saved their goods.

questions.stem: How is the whole passage organised?

options.text: it argues that fires are a good thing
it lists instructions for lighting a fire
it compares two different fires
it tells the events of the fire in the order they happened
it describes London as it is today

questions.explanation: The passage is a recount, moving in time from the outbreak to the rebuilding.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happened AFTER the wind at last dropped?

options.text: the fire spread across the river
the baker's shop first caught fire
the fire was halted and much of the old city lay in ashes
the Lord Mayor went back to bed
the long, dry summer began

questions.explanation: Only once the wind dropped was the fire halted, leaving much of the city in ashes.

questions.stem: Why does the writer include the story of the Lord Mayor going back to bed?

options.text: to show how one poor decision let the fire grow far worse
to prove that the Lord Mayor was simply tired
to make the reader laugh at bakers
to explain how firebreaks are built
to describe ordinary life in London

questions.explanation: The anecdote pins part of the disaster on a single bad decision, and the writer calls it 'a costly mistake'.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention Pepys burying his cheese and wine?

options.text: to prove that Pepys was greedy
to explain the best way to store cheese
to show that the fire was not serious
to give a vivid, memorable example of how people tried to save their belongings
to describe what Londoners usually ate

questions.explanation: The odd, human detail sticks in the mind and stands for all the Londoners scrambling to save what they could.

questions.stem: What is the writer's attitude to the fact that so few people died?

options.text: the writer treats it as a great tragedy
the writer doubts that it is true
the writer finds it dull and unimportant
the writer finds it surprising and worth pointing out
the writer blames it on the Lord Mayor

questions.explanation: The word 'remarkably' shows the writer is struck by how few lives were lost.

questions.stem: The passage ends with the new cathedral, designed by Sir Christopher Wren, rising where the old one fell. Why is this an effective ending?

options.text: it proves the fire never really happened
it shows something hopeful and lasting rising from the disaster
it warns readers never to visit London
it explains how cathedrals are built
it simply returns to the baker's shop

questions.explanation: Ending on the rebuilt cathedral turns the story from destruction towards renewal and hope.
